visuals.note: Size check first: 80 × 10 = 800, so the answer is more than 10x and less than 20x. Sofia's 1.5 lost a zero.

visuals.title: The rule of 72
visuals.formula: Years to double ≈ 72 ÷ annual growth rate (%)
visuals.note: 9% a year: about 8 years. 12%: about 6. Backwards: doubling in 3 years is about 24% a year.

visuals.at: Doubling in five years is an I-R-R
visuals.title: Annual return over five years
visuals.note: 72 ÷ 5 is about 14.5, so doubling in five years is an IRR of about 15%, not 20%.

visuals.title: Quiz
visuals.text: Five questions. Answer along on the cards below the transcript, then hear Marco's answers.

quiz.pause_at: Pause here if you want to think it through

questions.explain: 10% is 42, so 20% is 84. Take off 2%, about 8, and you get about 76.
questions.explain_at: Ten percent of four hundred and twenty is forty-two

questions.q: A company's margin rises from 20% to 25%. By how much has it risen?
questions.explain: It's five percentage points; as a percentage, 5 on a base of 20 is a quarter, so the margin is 25% higher.

questions.q: An investor doubles its money in five years. Roughly what annual return is that?
questions.explain: By the rule of 72, 72 ÷ 5 is about 14.5. Twenty percent is 100% spread over five years as simple interest, but returns compound.
questions.explain_at: Doubling in five years is an I-R-R of about fifteen percent

questions.q: GE Vernova pays $9bn at 13x Trench's adjusted EBITDA for 2028. Roughly what EBITDA does that imply?
questions.explain: 13 × 700 = 9,100, so $9bn ÷ 13 is a little under $700m. It matches 36% of about $1.9bn of revenue.
questions.explain_at: Thirteen times seven hundred is nine thousand one hundred

questions.q: GE Vernova says it's paying 13x EBITDA; Börsen-Zeitung's sources say about 21x. What explains most of the gap?

options.text: The 13x is in euros, not dollars

questions.explain: The 13x uses Trench's EBITDA for 2028, two years out. A growing company's future EBITDA is bigger, so the multiple looks smaller.
questions.explain_at: That's EBITDA two years from now
